Italian Citizens Favor Farm Artificial Intelligence While Expressing Notable Response Uncertainty

Italian citizens demonstrate moderate to high acceptance of artificial intelligence applications in agriculture, yet their favorable attitudes frequently coexist with measurable response uncertainty rather than fully established convictions, according to a nationwide survey published in Smart Agricultural Technology. Conducted by an interdisciplinary research team from institutions including the University of Turin, the investigation explored public attitudes toward eleven distinct artificial intelligence tools deployed across modern agri-food systems. Rather than treating public approval as a simple binary choice between acceptance and rejection, the study examined consumer evaluations as a behavioral continuum where positive sentiment can mask hesitation, ambivalence, or unfamiliarity. Using advanced statistical modeling that explicitly separates genuine preference from underlying decision-making uncertainty, the researchers found that acceptance indices consistently surpassed moderate thresholds across every evaluated technology. However, the degree of clarity with which respondents expressed their views varied widely depending on the specific application, individual educational attainment, household income, and participant age brackets.

The contemporary agricultural sector faces accelerating structural pressures to enhance overall productivity, safeguard environmental sustainability, and reinforce economic resilience against climate shocks and shifting market conditions. These multifaceted challenges serve as primary catalysts for sectoral digitalization, where advanced data-driven systems provide operational support for ongoing ecological and technological transitions toward sustainable food production models. In practical farming environments, modern agriculture must simultaneously manage soil functionality, monitor disease outbreaks, handle complex data streams, and address existing knowledge gaps separating primary producers from emerging technical innovations. Artificial intelligence, conceptualized in the investigation as the processing of massive operational datasets paired with sophisticated predictive algorithms, represents a prominent frontier for addressing these operational bottlenecks and reinforcing overall farm resilience. Through machine vision, autonomous machinery, and automated decision support systems, artificial intelligence allows producers to make informed agronomic choices, optimize field operations, and minimize adverse environmental impacts arising from conventional farming techniques.

Specific applications of artificial intelligence in agricultural practice encompass a diverse range of targeted technical interventions that optimize resource utilization across varied production environments. Autonomous systems can refine irrigation scheduling, guide the localized spraying of plant protection chemicals and herbicides, and streamline manual labor allocation to preserve soil quality while increasing operational efficiency. Processing agricultural data through machine learning and deep learning algorithms supports precision farming by creating increasingly autonomous systems capable of sensing ambient field conditions, learning from incoming measurements, and adapting functional routines. Previous empirical studies have demonstrated that automated equipment can manage field weeds without continuous human intervention, while drone imaging coupled with smart sensors enhances traceability and food supply chain sustainability. Nevertheless, while technical benefits such as real-time field monitoring, predictive equipment maintenance, and enhanced food safety management are widely discussed among industry experts, the extent to which everyday citizens understand and value these emerging agricultural technologies has remained largely unmeasured.

To evaluate public acceptance and perceived benefits among non-expert consumers, the research team designed an empirical survey administered through computer-assisted web interviewing between July and August 2025. Developed in collaboration with a specialized market research enterprise, the study protocol received formal ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of the University of Turin and adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki. The survey instrument underwent a rigorous two-stage pre-testing procedure, incorporating expert feedback from consumer science specialists and a pilot trial involving ten non-project participants to eliminate ambiguous phrasing or comprehension hurdles. Eligibility was restricted to adults aged 18 years or older residing in Italy, yielding 1,039 completed questionnaires with a completion rate of 96.10 percent. Following quality screening to remove 39 straight-line responses exhibiting identical Likert ratings across all survey items, the final analyzed sample comprised exactly 1,000 Italian citizens structured to reflect national demographic distributions across gender, age cohorts, household compositions, educational levels, and personal income tiers.

Participants evaluated eleven representative agricultural artificial intelligence technologies defined using self-constructed literature profiles: robotics and automation, drones and unmanned aerial vehicles, machine learning, convolutional neural networks, genetic algorithms, artificial neural networks, computer vision, digital twins, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, and big data analytics. Respondents rated their favorability toward each technology on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from not at all favorable to very favorable. Additionally, participants evaluated potential benefits across four predefined product dimensions: organoleptic and nutritional quality, contamination risk reduction and food safety, healthiness through reduced agrochemical residues, and environmental sustainability via resource efficiency and emissions cuts. To ensure uniform comprehension, respondents received standard reference sheets detailing each dimension. Rather than relying solely on conventional mean scores that conflate ambivalence with moderate favorability, the researchers analyzed acceptance using the Combination of Uniform and shifted Binomial model, known as the CUB framework, which disentangles preference intensity from decision uncertainty across ordinal response categories.

The statistical architecture of the CUB model decomposes observed ordinal responses into two distinct latent parameters bounded between zero and one: feeling, denoted by parameter xi, and response uncertainty, denoted by parameter pi. For direct interpretability, the researchers reported preference intensity as one minus xi and uncertainty as one minus pi, where higher values reflect stronger acceptance and elevated hesitation, respectively. The mathematical model exhibited satisfactory goodness-of-fit across all eleven technologies, with dissimilarity indices ranging from 0.06 to 0.10, well below the established 0.15 adequacy threshold. Overall findings demonstrated that consumer acceptance was universally moderate to high, with feeling values exceeding 0.70 across all tools, while response uncertainty generally remained below 0.50. The Internet of Things and machine learning attained the highest acceptance parameter of 0.81. However, the Internet of Things registered significantly lower response uncertainty at 0.29, compared to machine learning, indicating far more stable public evaluations.

In contrast to highly rated infrastructure tools, genetic algorithms recorded the lowest acceptance score among the evaluated items at 0.73, while digital twins generated the greatest response uncertainty at 0.39. Robotics and automation and computer vision occupied identical positions within the analytical space, exhibiting equivalent levels of estimated liking and uncertainty.
